full_judgment:
Refusal to grant reliefs to plaintiff Sreemati Hari Rani Basak by Courts below prompted her to knock at the door of this Court as petitioner on bestowing a Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure (for short the Code). Civil Revision Petition has been numbered as Civil Revision No. 380 of 1991.

2. Portrayal of intrinsic datum forming backdrop of Civil Revision Petition may succinctly be stated.

3. Sreemati Hari Rani Basak as plaintiff on 19-1-1979 instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 48 of 1979 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka seeking following reliefs:

a. A decree may be passed in favour of plaintiff and against defendants by confirming possession of plaintiff on "A" schedule property.

b. A decree for recovery of khas possession may be passed in favour of plaintiff and against defendants Nos. 4-12 in respect of "B" schedule property.

c. A decree may be passed in favour of plaintiff and against defendants by declaring that suit property cannot be treated as Vested and Non-resident Property.

d. A decree may be passed restraining defendants permanently not to disturb in any way plaintiff's possession in suit property.

4. Core contentions contended in plaint are:

a. Ramchandra Basak, Radhika Mohan Basak and Krishna Chandra Basak were rightful owners of suit property and their names had been correctly recorded in Cadastral Survey Khatian to the extent of 2 annas 13 gondas 1 kara 1 krantee share; 8 annas share and 5 annas, 6 gondas 2 karas and 2 krantes share respectively. Ramchandra Basak died leaving behind only son Madan Mohan Basak as his heir and Madan Mohan Basak became owner of 1/6 share of the property Radhika Mohan Basak, also, drew his last leaving behind only one son Gokul Chandra Basak as his only heir and Gokul Chandra Basak became owner of 1/2 share of property. Krishna Chandra Basak breathed his last leaving behind only son Kala Chand Basak as his only heir and Kala Chand Basak became rightful owner of 1/3 share of the property. Kala Chand Basak died leaving behind daughter Hari Rani Basak, the plaintiff, and Hari Rani Basak became owner to the extent of 1/3 share of property.

b. Suit property was put to auction in respect of property of Gokul Chandra Basak and Madan Mohan Basak and plaintiff purchased auction on 21-3-1939 through Court and got into possession of the auction purchased property. Plaintiff Hari Rani Basak by way of inheritance as well as auction purchase became 16 annas owner of suit property. Plaintiff Hari Rani Basak has been exercising acts of ownership and possession on suit property and her name had been correctly recorded in last Revisional Settlement Khatian as 16 annas owner and possessor of suit property. Plaintiff has been paying rent and got rent receipts.

c. Fourth-twelfth defendants were inducted as monthly tenants in a portion of Suit property by plaintiff and tenants defendants paid rents up to month of November, 1971, During War of Liberation of 1971, plaintiffs as well as tenants fourth-twelfth defendants left suit holding and took shelter on the other side of the border for safety of their lives. During the liberation movement plaintiff lost all counterfoils signed by tenants defendants and, also, some relevant title deeds and papers in respect of suit property. At the end of Liberation War plaintiff and fourth-twelfth defendants returned back to Bangladesh. Fourth-twelfth defendants took possession on portion of property as ejectable monthly tenants. Plaintiff demanded rent from tenants defendants defendants expressed their financial difficulty and requested plaintiff with folded hands to wait for some time. Fourth-twelfth defendants mounted endeavour to get lease of "B" schedule property from Assistant Custodian, Vested and Non-Resident Property disclosing that suit property is Vested and Non-Resident Property.

d. Cause of action of the suit arose on 17th September, 1978 when fourth-twelfth defendants refused to pay rent to plaintiff. Plaintiff, thus, had been constrained to present suit in Court on payment of ad valorem court fee on the valuation of suit which is Taka 50,000.

5. Third-defendant, Assistant Custodian of Vested Property contested the suit on presentation of a written statement pressing into service basic contentions:

a. Madan Mohan Basak, Gokul Chandra Basak and Kala Chand Basak had been exercising and enjoying case holding and they left Bangladesh with their family members in 1964 leaving the holding under care and custody of Dulal Chandra Basak, husband of plaintiff and cunning Dulal Chandra Basak taking advantage of long absence of original owners and their heirs adopted various devices to grab suit property which is purely an Enemy and Vested Property.

b. In Title Suit No. 195 of 1967 before Sixth Court of Munsif, Dhaka plaintiff took the stand that by amicable partition among other co-sharers she got 16 annas share of the holding but in the present suit she stated that she became the sole 16 annas owner and possessor of suit property by virtue of inheritance from her father Kala Chand Basal and, also, by way of auction purchase. Suit property is Enemy Property under Defence of Pakistan Rules of 1965. Plaintiff got no right, title and interest on the holding.

6. Fourth-twelfth defendants, also, laid a separate written statement, with similar averments as averred in written statement filed by third defendants except the stand not adopted by Third defendants but assumed by them that plaintiff is not the daughter of Kala Chand Basak and she is the daughter of one Krishna Chandra Basak who died leaving behind 3 sons who left for India in the year 1950. Defendants are in possession of suit property long before 1960. Under threat and coercion plaintiff's husband realised some money from some of defendants posing himself to be the owner of suit property without issuing any Rent Receipts and some of defendants paid money under mistaken belief that plaintiff's husband Dulal Chandra Basak was owner of suit property. Defendants became aware that suit property vested in Government as vested property and they applied for lease of suit property. Defendants became aware of a fraudulent suit and ex parte decree obtained by plaintiff and they laid Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 in the Sixth Court of Munsif, Dhaka for cancellation of decree.

7. Over pleadings learned Subordinate Judge framed following issues:

i. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

ii. Is the suit barred by limitation and hit by principles of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence.

iii. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

iv. Is the plaintiff entitled to get a decree for confirmation of possession on "A" schedule property, recovery of khas possession on "B" schedule property, permanent injunction and for declaration as prayed for?

8. Over pleadings and issues plaintiff and third-defendants fought out the suit. Fourth-twelfth defendants, though laid written statement, did not put up contest at the time of trial of suit. Evidence, both oral and documentary, had been led in support of respective contentions of plaintiff and third-defendant. Plaintiff examined two witnesses including herself as PW 1. Third-defendant placed on witness box one witness, DW 1 Tahshilder of Vested Property Cell in support of the case tabled by him. Fourth-twelfth defendants did not examine any witness in lending assurance to case put forth by them.

9. Learned Subordinate Judge as Trial Judge decided first, second and third issues in favour of plaintiff but decided fourth and fifth issues against plaintiff. In deciding fourth and fifth issues against plaintiff learned Trial Judge dismissed the suit Judgment and decree is dated 21-12-1986.

10. Plaintiff could not reconcile to above Judgment and decree and sought setting aside those through a medium of an appeal being Title Appeal No. 27 of 1987 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. Learned Additional District Judge, First Court Dhaka heard the appeal and by Judgment and Decree dated 14-10-1990 dismissed the appeal and maintained Judgment and Decree awarded by learned Trial Judge.

11. Feeling dissatisfied with appellate Judgment and Decree plaintiff Sreemati Hari Rani Basak as petitioner approached this Court in Civil Revision petition.

12. Sreemati Hari Rani Basak having breathed her last during pendency of Civil Revision her legal heirs had been substituted as petitioner Nos. 1(1)-1(10). Sreemati Hari Rani Basak shall be referred to hereinafter as plaintiff-petitioner. Substituted petitioners shall be described as petitioners. Third-defendant shall be known as third-defendant-opposite party. Fourth-twelfth defendants shall be described as fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties.

13. Petitioners submitted three Supplementary Affidavits incorporating some material facts and annexing some documents and papers as Annexures.

14. Second-defendant-Second opposite party Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), though did not lay any written statement, and, also, did not put up contest in the suit along with contesting third-defendant-opposite party filed Counter-Affidavit controverting statements made in Revision Petition.

15. Eleventh-defendant-eleventh-opposite party, also, though did not put up contest in the suit in spite of filing written statement along with other defendants- opposite parties, brought into existence Affidavit-in-opposition traversing statements embodied in Revision Petition.

16. Grounds pressed into service and contentions advanced from side of petitioners are catalogued hereunder:

i. Plaintiff-petitioner on oath having stated that she is the daughter of Kala Chand Basak, a co-sharer having 5 annas interest in suit property and contesting defendant having adduced no evidence contrary to that of plaintiff, Courts below committed an error of law in failing to hold that plaintiff is the daughter of Kala Chand Basak, and, plaintiff, as such, is entitled to a decree prayed for in the suit and by decisions of Courts below a failure of justice has been occasioned.

ii. Plaintiff-petitioner having asserted her source of title on inheritance as well as auction purchase of shares of other two co-sharers in the suit property, Courts below committed an error of law in failing to dispose of claim of plaintiff with reference to legal evidence on record and decisions of Courts below in dismissing the suit of plaintiff suffers from a gross illegality and legal infirmity and a failure of justice has been occasioned to plaintiffs-petitioners.

iii. Courts below committed an error of law in holding in summary way that certified copies produced by plaintiff in support of purchase of 2/3rd share of suit property in an auction sale are forged which is contrary to Rule of Procedure in determination of documents and by the illegal decisions of Courts below on a material evidence, a failure of justice has been occasioned.

iv. Plaintiff 'having not been confronted under section 145 of the Evidence Act in respect of her claim on suit property on the basis of a partition between co-sharers, Courts below fell into an error in drawing an adverse inference against her in the suit in hand on her previous alleged claim and by decisions of Courts below a failure of justice had been occasioned.

v. Tenants-defendants having challenged the decree obtained by plaintiff in Title Suit No. 195 of 1967 on institution of a suit being Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 and having failed there, Courts below erred in law in failing to consider that Judgment and Decree recorded in the aforesaid suit are relevant in passing a decree in the instant suit filed by plaintiff.

vi. Plaintiff having obtained a decree of permanent injunction against Government as well as the tenants prior to the declaration of suit property as Vested Property, courts below committed a substantial error is not holding that the property is not Vested Property.

vii. Government is not entitled to set up tenants on suit property until there is a partition of the same in between plaintiff and Government and failure on the part of Courts below to determine the points led to a failure of Justice.

Jagannath (Plaintiff) vs Baldeo (Defendant) 1883 ILR Vol. V page 305 Allahabad Series (FB) Tara Prasad Mytee vs Nund Kishore Giri and others ILR 1883 Vol. IX Calcutta Series, 842, Naigar Timapa vs Bhaskar Parmaya and another ILR 1886, Bombay Series 444, Abul Khair Miah being dead his heirs Abul Kashem and others vs Bangladesh and others 32 DLR (AD) 29, Sunil Kumar Ghosh and others vs Bangladesh and others, 1988 BLD 131 and Aroti Rani Paul vs Sudarshan Kumar Paul 56 DLR (AD) 73 have been relied upon in aid of contentions advanced.

17. Contentions so surged forward have been repelled from side of opposite parties on raising counter-contentions which are as follows:

i. There had been no error occurred in initiation of Vested Property proceeding in respect of suit property. DW 1 Tahshilder made an enquiry on the spot and on the basis of enquiry Vested Property proceedings had been started and there had been no illegality in Vested Property proceeding. DW 1 furnished version in proof of legality of Vested property proceeding.

ii. Findings reached by learned Trial Judge rested upon proper assessment and appreciation of evidences and material on record which were maintained by Appellate Judge and findings recorded by Courts below are immune from attack in exercise of Revisional Authority envisaged in section 115 of The Code.

18. In the face of evidences, materials on record and rival contentions advanced from the side of petitioners and opposite parties pivotal points which outlast for determination are or, to put it differently, destiny of Civil Revision hinges on answers to the following points.

i. Whether plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak had been grand-daughter of Krishna Mohan Basak and daughter of Kala Chand Basak.

ii. Whether plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak auction purchased property in auction sale and whether her title passed by way of auction purchase.

iii. Whether defendants-opposite parties could lay any legal evidence in respect of loss of domicile in origin of Krishna Chandra Basak and Kalachand Basak and whether suit property could and can be brought under mischief of former Enemy property now vested property.

iv. Whether plaintiff-petitioner is entitled to a decree of confirmation of possession in respect of property described in schedule 'A' to plaint and recovery of khas possession against fourth-twelfth defendants in respect of schedule 'B' property of plaint.

v. Whether plaintiff-petitioner is entitled to a decree of permanent injunction against fourth-twelfth defendant-opposite parties restraining the latter permanently from disturbing in any way plaintiff-petitioners' possession over suit property.

vi. Whether Judgments under challenge in Civil Revision case can be sustained on evidence, materials on record, fact and circumstances of case and, also, in safe dispensation of Civil Justice.

19. Points formulated are being broached and riposted.

20. Point No. 1: Case projected by plaintiff in the plaint is that Krishna Chandra Basak was owner of suit property to the extent of 5 annas, 6 gondas 2 karas, and 2 krantes share and Krishna Chandra Basak died leaving behind only son Kala Chand Basak and Kala Chand Basak breathed his last leaving behind Hari Rani Basak, plaintiff as only heir. Third-defendant-third-opposite party Assistant Custodian of Vested Property in written statement admitted that Krishna Chandra Basak died leaving behind son Kala Chand Basak. Third Defendant-opposite party in written statement did not programme any case that plaintiff Hari Rani Basak is not daughter of Kala Ctiond Basak. Fourth-twelfth defendants in 11(e) paragraph of written statement asserted that plaintiff is not daughter of Kala Chand Basak, rather she is daughter of one Krishna Chandra Basak. Plaintiff Hari Rani Basak standing on witness box in support of case put forth in the plaint provided version that her father Kala Chand Basak died leaving behind her as only daughter and she is legal heir of her father. Further evidence is that the name of her grandfather is Krishna Chandra Basak and her grandfather died leaving behind her father Kala Chand Basak as the only son. Evidence is produced hereunder:

আমার পিতা কারাচান বসাক আমাকে একমাত্র কন্যা রাখিয়া এই বাংলাদেশেই মৃত্যুবরণ করেন। আমি আমার পিতার একমাত্র কন্যা ও ওয়ারিশ। আমার ঠাকুর দাদার নাম কৃষ্ণ চন্দ্র বসাক এবং আমার ঠাকুর দাদা আমার পিতা কালাচান বসাককে একমাত্র পুত্র রাখিয়া পরলোক গমন করেন।

In cross-examination, plaintiff PW 1 Hari Rani Basak asserted that name of her father is Kala Chand Basak and name of her grandfather is Krishna Chandra Basak and her father drew his last leaving her as the only heir and she inherited 5 annas 6 gondas 2 karas and 2 Krantes share as heir from her father. Testimony, in cross-examination, is extracted hereunder:

আমার বাবা আমাকে একমাত্র ওয়ারিশ রাখিয়া পরলোক গমন করেন। আমার বাবার আর কোন ভাই ছিল না।

Evidence offered by plaintiff PW 1 in examination-in-chief could not be at all blown to smithereens by way of cross-examination from the side of contesting third-defendant-opposite party rather version provided by her in examination-in-chief stood cemented in cross-examination. DW 1, Tahshilder standing on witness box in support of case put forth by third-defendant opposite party, Assistant Custodian of Vested Property did not utter a single word that plaintiff PW 1 Hari Rani Basak is neither grand-daughter of Krishna Chandra Basak nor daughter of Kala Chand Basak.

21. Rule 3 of Order VIII enshrines: It shall not be sufficient for a defendant in his written statement to deny generally the grounds alleged by the plaintiff, but the defendant must deal specifically with each allegation of fact of which he does not admit the truth, except damages. Rule 5 of Order VIII postulates: Every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability: Provided that the Court may, in its discretion, require any fact so admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admission. Mandate of rule 5 of Order VIII is that unless allegation of fact contained in the plaint is not specifically denied, that allegation of fact shall be taken to be admitted. Since third-defendant opposite-party did not put forward any specific denial in respect of statement of fact in the plaint that she is the grand-daughter of Krishna Chandra Basak and daughter of Kala Chand Basak that statement shall stand treated as admitted by third-defendant-opposite party.

22. Fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite-parties though, in 11(e) paragraph of written statement tabled the case that plaintiff is not daughter of Kala Chand Basak rather, she is daughter of Krishna Chandra Basak, did not at all enter their appearance during trial and did not examine themselves nor did produce any witness in support of the said contention contended in 11(e) paragraph of written statement. Evidence provided by plaintiff as PW 1 in respect of her heirship from her father Kala Chand Basak could be endeavoured to be flung to the winds by way of cross-examination from side of fourth-twelfth defendants but plaintiff PW 1 was not at all cross-examined from side of fourth-twelfth defendants. Cross-examination of a witness is the greatest legal engine for discovery of the truth. Cross-examination is directed to bring to light truth by clarifying matters which a witness may deserve to keep concealed. Failure on the part of fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties to cross-examine plaintiff PW 1 definitely raises presumption and legal inference that evidence provided by plaintiff PW 1 in examination-in-chief has been accepted by fourth-twelfth defendants. Support for the proposition of law is sought to be drawn from authoritative observation of  Lord Chancellor Herschell in the case of Browne vs Dunn (1983)6, R 67, AEG Carapiet vs AY Derderain, 1961 Calcutta 359 DB and Nur Mohammad and another vs Sultan Ahmed and another, 40 DLR 369.

23. Authoritative observation of Lord Chancellor Hershell in the case of Browne vs Dunn (Supra) has been couched in the following language:

"Now my Lords, I cannot help saying that it seems to me to be absolutely essential to the proper conduct of a cause where it is intended to suggest that a witness is not speaking the truth on a particular point, to direct his attention to the fact, by some questions put in cross-examination showing that imputation is intended to be made, and not to take his evidence and pass it by as a matter altogether unchallenged and then, when it is possible for him to explain, as perhaps he might have been able to do if such questions had been put to him, the circumstances which it is suggested indicate that the story he tells ought not to be believed, to argue that he is a witness unworthy of credit Mr Lords, I have always understood that if you intend to impeach a witness give are bound, whilst he is in the box, to give him an opportunity of making any explanation which is open to him, and as it seems to me, that is not only a rule of professional practice in the conduct of a case, but is essential to fair play and fair dealing with witness."

24. In AEG Carapiet vs AY Derderain (Supra) it has been laid down

"Wherever the opponent has declined to avail himself of the opportunity to put his essential and material case in cross-examination, it must follow that he believed that the testimony given could not be disputed at all. It is wrong to think that this is merely a technical rule of evidence. It is a rule of essential justice."

25. In Nur Mohammad and another vs Sultan Ahmed and another (Supra) it has been held:

"It is a well settled principle of law regarding cross examination that on failure of a party to cross-examine the witness of his adversary appearing against him on material evidence it will be presumed by Court that testimony given by that witness-in-chief has been accepted as it cannot be suggested that his statement on a particular fact is untrue unless he is cross-examined drawing his attention to that fact and thereby giving him an opportunity to explain the same. This rule of cross-examination is not merely "a technical rule of evidence" but it is as well "a rule of essential justice" because it is essential to fair play and fair dealing with witnesses."

26. Fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite-party, though, had the opportunity, of cross-examining plaintiff PW 1, did not participate in the peremptory hearing of suit and did not cross-examine plaintiff PW 1 and version supplied by plaintiff PW 1 remained unimpeached and un-assailed and the same stands admitted by fourth-twelfth defendants.

27. This takes me to another vital aspect touching the war of words engrossed in point No. 1. Admittedly, fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties as plaintiff instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 in the Sixth Court of Munsif at Dhaka for declaration that ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 195 of 1967 is void, fraudulent, inoperative illegal and not binding upon plaintiffs. In the plaint, plaintiff-petitioner Sreemati Hari Rani Basak had been depicted as daughter of Kala Chand Basak, resident of 26, Mohajanpur Lane, Police Station Sutrapur, Dhaka. In the face of showing plaintiff-petitioner Sreemati Hari Rani Basak as daughter of Kala Chand Basak it does not lie in the mouth of fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties to install the case that plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak is not the daughter of Kala Chand Basak and fourth-twelfth defendants are bound by their admission and they stand estopped/precluded to say that plaintiff is not the daughter of Kala Chand Basak.

28. Learned Trial Judge as well as Appellate Judge failed to take into account evidence offered by plaintiff as PW 1 which remained unassailed and unimpeached both from the side of third-defendant opposite party and fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties. Learned Trial Judge committed a substantial error in holding that plaintiff did not examine any witness to prove herself as a daughter of Kala Chand Basak and she has failed to produce any document to that effect and RS Khatian stands in the name of Dulal Chandra Basak. Learned Trial Judge totally ignored the factual aspect that plaintiff as PW 1 examined herself in support of the claim that she is the daughter of Kala Chand Basak and her testimony in this regard could not be shattered nor impeached by way of cross-examination from the side of third-defendant opposite party. Learned Trial Judge fell into a patent error in holding that by her (plaintiff) failure to adduce sufficient evidence to that effect cloud of doubt was naturally peeping through the horizon of their mind. Finding reached by Trial Judge perilously borders on perversity. Learned Trial Judge, also, failed to take into grip that in Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties had been plaintiffs and in plaint they described Hari Rani Basak as the daughter of Kala Chand Basak. Learned Appellate Judge, also, committed the same error in finding that no documentary evidence had been produced in Court in proof that plaintiff was daughter of CS recorded tenant Kala Chand Basak. Learned Appellate Judge, also, committed a grave error in taking into account the unfounded and unjustified doubt put into words by learned Trial Judge in the decision. Learned Appellate Judge, also, was in patent error in holding that plaintiff could not produce any documentary evidence in trial Court that she is the daughter of Cadastral Survey recorded tenant Kalachand Basak. Kalachand Basak was not the recorded tenant of Cadastral Survey Record of Right rather, his father Krishna Chandra Basak was Cadastral Survey recorded tenant and this is a manifestation of non-application of mind on the part of learned Appellate Judge, Learned Appellate Judge did not at all come to take into stock plaint of Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 wherein Hari Rani Basak was portrayed as daughter of Kalachand Basak and plaint of Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 is a vital documentary evidence in proof of case projected by plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak that she is daughter of Kala Chand Basak.

29. In the discourse made above, the irresistible conclusion that can be drawn is that plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak is granddaughter or Krishna Chandra Basak and daughter of Kala Chand Basak.

30. Point No. 1, thus, stands decided in the epithet that plaintiff-petitioner Sreemati Hari Rani Basak is grand-daughter of Krishna Chandra Basak and daughter of Kala Chand Basak.

31. Point No. 2: Plaintiff-petitioner asserted that share to the extent of 10 annas 13 gondas 1 kara and 1 krantee owned by Gokul Chandra Basak and Madan Mohan Basak had been put to auction in Money Decree Execution Case No. 17 of 1938 arising out of Money Suit No. 6 of 1935 and auction was purchased by her on 11-3-1939. Third-defendant-opposite party in seventh paragraph of written statement only offered a denial in respect of the statement made in sixth paragraph of plaint and outlined the said statement made in that paragraph to be forged. It was only stated that to grab Vested Property collusive papers had been prepared. Positive case had been programmed in ninth paragraph of written statement. No specific case had been tabled that there had not been any auction in respect of shares of Madan Mohan Basak and Gokul Chandra Basak. Plaintiff PW 1 furnished version that she became owner of suit property by way of inheritance to the extent of 5 annas 6 gondas 2 karas, 2 krantes share and by way of auction purchase to the extent of 10 annas 13 gondas 1 kara 1 krantee share. She provided account that through Court she got possession of auction purchased property. She submitted Sale Certificate, Exhibit 3 and Writ of Delivery of Possession, Exhibit 3A and Suit Register, Exhibit 3(b) evidencing that shares of Madan Mohan Basak and Gokul Basak had been put to auction in Money Decree Execution Case No. 17 of 1938 arising out of a Money Suit No. 6 of 1935. Evidence offered by her in examination-in-chief was affirmed in cross-examination from the side of third-defendant-opposite party and auction purchase matter could neither be at all shattered nor discredited nor impeached by way of any sort of cross-examination from side of defendant-opposite parties. It had earlier been stated that fourth-twelfth Defendant abstained in participating in trial of the suit and did not produce any witness in support of statements contained in their written statement and statement made in written statement had not been at all substantiated.

32. Exhibit 3(b) is certified copy of Suit Register of Money Suit No. 6 of 1935. Suit Register demonstrates that process under Order XXI, rule 54 of The Code had been issued on 28-6-1938 and had been duly served on 14-8-1938. Notice under Order XXI, rule 66 of The Code had been issued on 23-9-1939. Sale Proclamation had been published on 12-12-1938. Sale took place on 21-3-1939 and it was purchased by Hari Rani Basak, daughter of Kala Chand Basak, 26 Mahajonpur, Sutrapur; Dhaka through her Pleader RK Bhoumik for Rupees 5,693. Sale had been confirmed on 20-4-1939. Process under Order XXI, rule 95 of The Code had been issued on 18-5-1939. Possession had been delivered on 8-6-1939 and Execution case stood disposed of with full satisfaction on 15-7-1939. Exhibit 3 is Certificate of Sale of property under Order XXI, rule 94 of The Code, Sale Certificate, Exhibit 3 manifests that plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak, daughter of Kalachand Basak, purchased auction at Taka 5,693 and sale was confirmed on 20-4-1939. Exhibit 3A is Writ of Delivery of Possession under Order XXI, rule 95 of The Code. Writ of delivery of possession manifests that plaintiff Hari Rani Basak, daughter of Kala Chand Basak, purchased the auction and remained auction purchaser-owner and possession of auction purchased property had been handed over to auction purchaser Hari Rani Basak through process of Court. Exhibits 3(b), 3 and 3(a) are documents revealing that property to the extent of 10 annas 5 gondas 1 Kara 1 krantee share owned by Gokul Chandra Basak and Madan Mohan Basak had been put to auction and plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak purchased property of the above shares i.e. 2/3 of share of the whole property and sale was confirmed. Sale Certificate had been issued and on the strength of Writ of Delivery of Possession, auction purchaser plaintiff PW 1 Hari Rani Basak had entered into possession through process of law.

33. Learned Trial Judge in the Judgment held that defendant-Government had categorically stated that so-called auction purchase, Certificate of Sale and Writ of Delivery of Possession were forged and created only to grab the property. Careful examination of written statement laid by third-defendant-opposite party indicated that statement embodied in Sixth paragraph of plaint in regard to auction sale and purchase of property had been denied in Seventh paragraph of written statement in the language that statements in Sixth paragraph of plaint are false and got up story and to grab the property. Learned Trial Judge took into account Articles 217 and 218(1) of Civil Rules and Orders and held that there was no scope to issue any certified copy of Certificate of Sale by Civil Court and, thus, came to the finding that certified copy of the same was definitely a forged one and papers of alleged auction purchase were created purposefully Learned Appellate Judge, also, taking into stock Articles 217 and 218(1) of Civil Rules and Orders Volume-1 adopted view that certified copy of Sale Certificate could not be issued by civil Court, inasmuch as certified copy of Sale Certificate was to be transmitted to Office of Registrar and ultimately held, that certified copy of Sale Certificate was not legally acceptable. Learned Appellate Judge, also, found that certified copy of Suit Register by open eyes appeared to be improper. Learned Appellate Judge, also, found that from original record, which was called for, nothing could be found in respect of filing of a Money Suit.

34. On a careful examination of certified copy of Money Suit Register nothing wrong, no illegality and nothing improper could be detected. Article 217 of Civil Rules and Orders Volume I enjoins that Sale Certificate shall be made over/handed over to party applying for it and it shall be certified to be true copy and forwarded to Registry Office without delay. True it is that Exhibit 3, certified copy of Sale Certificate, was not done by Registry Office but from Civil Court. Plaintiff-petitioner in Supplementary Affidavit annexed photocopy of certified copy of Sale Certificate as Annexure-Z-16 and that Sale Certificate is issued by Sub-Registrar, Sadar Record Room, Dhaka. Learned Counsel for plaintiff-petitioner produced before me certified copy of the said Sale Certificate. The certified copy of the Sale Certificate had been obtained on 25-10-1993. A careful comparison of certified copy of Sale Certificate, Exhibit 3 issued from Civil Court and Certified Copy of Sale Certificate issued by Sub-Registrar, Sadar Record Room, Dhaka manifests that two copies of Sale Certificates are exactly the same. Issuance of a certified copy from Civil Court may be an irregular act but by that irregular act it cannot be at all suggested that Sale Certificate is a forged and created one.

35. Leaving aside Sale Certificate there are other documents in support of auction purchase by plaintiff-petitioner Hari Rani Basak. The concept of "Enemy" and "Enemy Property" were offspring of Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965 (XXIII of 1965) and Rules framed thereunder. Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and Rules framed thereunder made by Central Government of Pakistan in exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of The Ordinance are reproduction of Defence of India Act and Rules of 1939 made under the Act. On 6-9-1965 Emergency was proclaimed by the then President of the then Pakistan who declared that grave emergency existed and Pakistan was in eminent danger of being threatened by war. Further declaration was that Pakistan was at war with India. In pursuance of Declaration of Emergency the then President of Pakistan promulgated Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965 (XXIII of 1965). In exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of the Ordinance, Central Government framed Rules, which are called The Defence of Pakistan Rules. In exercise of power conferred by Rule 182 of Defence of Pakistan Rules, which is contained in Part XVI of aforesaid Rules dealing with Enemy Property, empowers the Government to promulgate order and prescribe thereby the doing of certain acts by custodian as stipulated in clauses (a) and (f).

46. In sub-rule 2 of Rule 2 of The Defence of Pakistan Rules the expression "Enemy" has been defined as hereunder:

"Enemy" means any person or State at war with Pakistan.

In sub-rule 3 of Rule 2 "Enemy Territory" has been coined as follows:

Any area which is under the sovereignty of or administered by or for the time being in the occupation of a State at war with Pakistan.

In Rule 161 of The Defence of Pakistan Rules the expression "Enemy" had been stated in the following way:

(a)	any State or sovereign of State at war with Pakistan or

(b) any individual resident in any enemy territory.

Sub-rule 1 of Rule 169 defines any Enemy subject as hereunder:

(a) any individual who possesses the Nationality of State at War with Pakistan or having possessed such Nationality at any time has lost it without acquiring another Nationality.

Sub-rule 4 of Rule 169 defines "Enemy property" as follows:

"Enemy Property" means any property for the time being belonging to or held or managed on behalf of an enemy as defined in rule 161, an enemy subject or an enemy firm, but does not include property which is "evacuee property" under the Pakistan "Administration of Evacuee Property Act."

58. The word "Domicile" is derived from Latin word "Domus" meaning home or dwelling house. "Domicile" is the legal conception of Home and the term "Home" is frequently used in defining or describing the legal concept of Domicile. In Corpus Juris Secundum 28 page 3 it is stated:

Domicile is the relation which the law creates between an individual and a particular locality or country. What has been said to be the most comprehensive and correct definition which could be given is that in a strict legal sense the domicile of a person is the place where he has true, fixed, permanent home and principal establishment and to which, whenever he is absent, he has the intention of returning.

59. In Bell vs Kennedy (1868) LR 1 HL 307 it has been laid down:

60. In Winans and another vs Attorney-General (1904) AC 287 the question of loss of domicile of origin of a citizen came up for consideration. It has been held:

The onus of proving that a domicile has been chosen in substitution for the domicile of origin lies upon those who assert that the domicile of origin has been lost. The domicile of origin continues unless a fixed and settled intention of abandoning the first domicile and acquiring another as the sole domicile is clearly shown.

Observation of Lord Halsbury, in the case, has been couched in the following terms:

The law is plain, that where a domicile of origin is proved, lies upon the person who asserts a change of domicile to establish it.

61. The question of loss of domicile came up before the Allahabad High Court in Abida Khatoon and another vs State of UP and others, AIR 1963 Allahabad 260. Observation of Dhawan, J. has been coined in the following language:

Citizenship does not evaporate with the passing of time; it clings to a person wherever he may roam. It cannot be taken away from him, unless he voluntarily renounces it or is guilty of some conduct involving loss of citizenship. The onus of proving that a citizen of India has lost his citizenship is on the party seeking to deprive him of his rights as a citizen.

Further observation is in the following terms:

To every adult person the law assigns a domicile which is called the domicile of origin and which remains attached to him until a new and different domicile takes its place. The domicile of origin must prevail until the party has not only manifested but carried into execution an intention of abandoning his former domicile and acquiring another as his sole domicile.

In the suit in hand i.e. Title Suit No. 48 of 1979, fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties in Eleventh (F) paragraph positively put into words that plaintiff's husband is a dangerous and desperate man and under threat and coercion he realised some money from some of defendants posing himself to be owner of suit property without issuing any rent receipts and some of defendants paid money under mistaken belief that plaintiff's husband Dulal Chandra Basak was the owner of suit property. By this proclamation in Eleventh (f) paragraph of written statement, fourth-twelfth-defendants again admitted themselves to be tenants under plaintiff. There could not arise any occasion/ground on the part of these defendants to pay money to husband of plaintiff unless the latter is the rightful owner-landlord of suit premises. The words "mistaken belief" has been introduced only for a malafide and ulterior motive. From the statement incorporated in plaint of Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 and, also, written statement laid in the present Title Suit No. 48 of 1979 fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties depicted themselves as tenants under Plaintiff-Petitioner Hari Rani Basak.

78. It has been earlier noticed that in Enemy Property case record no order could be found by which it can be said that fourth-twelfth-Defendants had been granted lease in some portion of suit property. Annexure-B series are simply applications for renewal of lease and those applications were dated 23-1-1985. But there is nothing evidencing that lease had been renewed in their favour. It is posited here that since there had not been any order of lease in favour of fourth-twelfth-defendants, question of renewal of lease in their favour did not and does not arise at all.

79. Eleventh-Defendant-Opposite Party, though, by way of Affidavit-in-opposition annexed some House Rent Receipts dated 3-5-2006; 2-7-2006, 31-7-2006 and 5-11-2006 respectively showing payment of lease money from1981-2005, those House Rent Receipts are in the name of one Jogesh Chandra Das and not in the name of Eleventh-Defendant-opposite party Anil Chandra Mondal. Eleventh-Defendant-opposite party Anil Chandra Mondal, thus, could not show any House Rent Receipt allegedly granted to him by Vested Property Authority. It had been earlier voiced that fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties did not put up contest at the time of trial and did not substantiate the case put forward by them in written statement and they, also, did not enter appearance in the appeal. Eleventh, third-tenth and twelfth-defendants had been impleaded as opposite parties in Civil Revision case as a matter of procedure as because they were defendants in the suit. Eleventh-Defendant-opposite party got no legal character and locus standi to appear in Civil Revision case on laying an Affidavit-in-opposition.

80. Sub-Article 3 of Article 4 of East Pakistan (Land and Buildings) Administration Disposal Order, 1966 enshrines that notwith-standing anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any agreement, a person to whom any property is leased out or let out under sub-paragraph (2) shall not acquire any right of occupation in such property and shall not be entitled to hold over after the expiry of period of lease. None of defendant-opposite parties could show by any documentary evidence that lease had been granted to them and the same had been renewed from year to year. Eleventh-Defendant-opposite party, who entered appearance in Civil Revision case by way of an Affidavit-in-opposition, also, could not produce House Rent Receipts since the year 1966 and House Rent Receipts annexed in Affidavit-in-opposition was of one Jogesh Chandra Das and those were for the year 1981-2005. Eleventh-Defendant-opposite party and others do not have any leasehold right over suit property and their status are ejectable tenants under plaintiff-petitioner.

81. In Arti Rani Paul vs Sudarshan Kumar Paul and others 56 DLR (AD) 73 appellant as plaintiff instituted a suit being Other Suit No. 206 of 1997 before Court of Subordinate Judge, Dinajpur for declaration of her title in the suit land and, also, for further declaration that order passed by Second-Defendant Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dinajpur on 12-10-1976 in VP Case No. 15(JA)FU/76-77 treating suit property as vested property is illegal, void and not binding upon plaintiff. Trial Court decreed the suit holding that second-defendant illegally treated the suit property as vested property. Against the decree neither Government nor Vested Property authority preferred an appeal challenging the said decree but only alleged year-to-year lease holders preferred an appeal, though, they had no locus standi to challenge the aforesaid Judgment and Decree of trial Court. Learned Additional District Judge as Appellate Judge dismissed the appeal and maintained Judgment and Decree of Trial Judge. On a Revision before the High Court Division concurrent decisions of Courts below stood set aside. Leave to Appeal was presented before the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division held:

Neither the Government nor Vested Property authority challenged the decree of trial Court and it is defendant Nos. 6-8 being lessees of Vested property for one year cannot have any locus standi to challenge the decree or prefer an appeal against such decree. It is for the Vested Property authority to challenge the decree. The defendant Nos. 6-8 being year-to-year lease holders have no locus standi to prefer an appeal before appellate Court as well as in the High Court Division and, as such, learned Single Judge of the High Court Division having failed to consider this aspect of the case, committed an error of law which resulted in an error in the decision causing failure of justice.

<u>82. The case in hand is worse than the case quoted above. In the case in hand, defendant-opposite parties including Eleventh-Defendant-opposite party did neither put up contest in the suit nor did substantiate the case designed in written statement nor did enter appearance in the appeal and only in Revision stage being not at all a lessee and having not got any leasehold right on way portion of suit property participated in the hearing of Revision case. I am of this considered view that Eleventh-Defendant-opposite party even if he had been made an opposite party in Civil Revision Petition is neither a lessee nor had/ has any leasehold right on any portion of suit property and he did not have any locus standi nor any legal character to appear in Revision case.</u>

<u>83. Evidence and materials on record demonstrate that fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties having entered into a portion of suit property as tenants under plaintiff-petitioner in a malafide way, engineered and hatched up a conspiracy to cement their illegal and unauthorized occupation on suit property and are mounting strives to have lease of suit property getting the property treated as Enemy Property and by their conduct and character they characterized themselves as hostile, tenants and their conduct demands their eviction from suit property. It is conveniently observed that now-a-days, specially in Metropolitan cities and urban areas, there is  a tendency on the part of persons who having been inducted into possession of premises/house/building as a tenant, litigate and consume time as an umbrella for continuation of illegal possession thereon. The case in hand is a glaring paradigm how fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties launched endeavour to prolong their illegal occupation on suit property. This type of tendency on the part of fourth-twelfth defendants must be curbed.</u>

<u>84. Learned Trial Judge failed to take into stock relevant provision of law in respect of vesting a property as Enemy Property and he totally misdirected himself in his approach in resolving the war of words and committed a substantial error in arriving at a finding that original owners left this country in 1964 and in their absence plaintiff, belonging to the same community, adopted various devices to grab suit property which was purely an Enemy Property. Appellate Judge as last Judge of fact was duty bound to come to a finding on discussion on materials on record, whether the predecessor grandfather Krishna Chandra Basak and father Kala Chand Basak were Enemies and whether the property could be brought under the mischief of Enemy Property laws and whether treating of property as Enemy Property suffered from illegality, but Appellate Judge did not at all touch the vital issue involved in the case and, thus, committed a grave error of law by which a failure of justice has been occasioned.</u>

85. In the view of discourse Made above, 1 am of this considered and dispassionate view that neither. Kalachand Basak nor plaintiff-petitioner Sreemati Hari Rani Basak were and are Enemies and suit property is not Enemy property and Enemy Property Proceeding and Enemy Property case in respect of suit property is illegal, void, ultra vires and without jurisdiction and the suit property cannot be at all brought under the mischief of former Enemy Property now Vested Property proceeding.

86. Point No. 3 is decided in the terms that defendants-opposite parties could not lay any legal evidence in respect of loss of domicile in origin of Krishna Chandra Basak and Kala Chand Basak and suit property could not be and cannot be brought under the mischief of former Enemy Property now Vested Property.

87. 88. On a careful assessment of pleadings, evidences, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case the irresistible conclusion that can be drawn is that plaintiff-petitioner could successfully prove her right, title and possession on suit property and plaintiffs petitioner is entitled to get decree of confirmation of possession on 'A' Schedule property and, also, for a decree of recovery of khas possession against fourth-twelfth-defendants in respect of 'B' Schedule property.

89. Point No. 4 stands ruled out in the terms that plaintiff-petitioner is entitled to a decree of confirmation of possession in respect of property described in schedule 'A' and recovery of khas possession in schedule 'B' property to the plaint.

90. Point No. 5 is resolved in epithet that plaintiff-petitioner is entitled to a decree of Permanent Injunction against fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties and fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite party are restrained by a decree of Permanent Injunction from disturbing in any way plaintiff's petitioner's possession over suit property.

92. Point No. 6: In view of discourse made in foregoing paragraphs the insurmountable verdict that can be proclaimed is that decisions reached by Learned Trial Judge and Appellate Judge do not at all claim any justification as those are not backed by legal evidence, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case. There had been misconstruction and misreading of material documents and total misdirection in the approach on the part of Learned Trial Judge and Appellate Judge in resolving legal controversies. Decisions suffer from sheer waywardness, gross illegality, legal infirmity and grave error of law.
